elements.content: Grammar focus: Ellipsis & Substitution.

Delete what a reader can restore without a second reading, and substitute when the deletion would leave two possible readings. Keep the auxiliary, the negative and any contrasting element: they carry the meaning the deletion would otherwise lose.

auxiliary stranded — keeps tense and polarity visible: others did not / he has
do so / do it — substitutes a verb phrase: they promised a review and did so
one / ones — substitutes a countable noun: the second one, the cheaper ones
so / not — substitutes a whole clause: if so, I think not
former / latter — orders two named items: the former, the latter
to (infinitive ellipsis) — avoids repeating the verb: I meant to, but I didn't
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Complete: 'She asked for the file, and I sent ___.'
2. Complete: 'The older models failed; the newer ___ held.'
3. Which is the correct elliptical reply?
options: He said he would come, and he did.
He said he would come, and he came did.

elements.content: Read and listen: three examples in context.

Noun — Some members accepted the terms; others did not. (The auxiliary survives, the verb goes.)
Substitution — The first draft was rejected and the second one never reached the board. (One replaces a countable noun.)
Clause — It may rain; if so, we meet online. (So replaces a whole clause.)
What do you observe?

Ellipsis deletes words that the context restores: others did not [accept the terms]. Substitution replaces them with a pro-form when deletion would be ambiguous: the second one stands for the second proposal, do so stands for a repeated verb phrase, so stands for a whole clause. Auxiliaries usually survive ellipsis, which is why did not remains after the main verb disappears.
1. What does 'the second one' replace?
2. Which part typically survives ellipsis?
State the rule in one sentence, without looking at the table.
Freer production: Can analyze AI ethics and data privacy frameworks while maintaining high stylistic cohesion

Success criteria:
- I can drop a repeated verb phrase and keep the auxiliary.
- I can use one and do so instead of repeating a noun or a verb.
- I can use so and not to stand for a whole clause.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ Others did not accepted the terms (auxiliary and verb both half-kept) → ✅ Others did not accept the terms
❌ They promised a review and they delivered (verb repeated, object dropped) → ✅ They promised a review and they delivered one
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

The first draft was rejected and the second one never reached the board.
Some accepted the terms; most did not.
It may rain; if so, we meet online.
